The wording is exact and the chapter is right. The page reference to the Penguin Modern Classics printing of 2001 could not be checked against a copy, so it is dropped and the first edition is named instead. The feast is the one Okonkwo gives his mother’s kinsmen in Mbanta at the end of his exile.

Corrected the locator. Watching the Reapers is poem 15 of the whole volume, not the fifteenth poem of the Po Chu-i section, where it stands fifth. In the happiness of his subjects lies his happiness; in their welfare his welfare; whatever pleases himself he shall not consider as good, but whatever pleases his subjects he shall consider as good.

The locator named the Bangalore Government Press, which published the translation, in the place of the translator. The wording is R. Shamasastry’s and is verified at Book I, chapter XIX. Authorship and date are traditional: scholars treat the text as composite and place its compilation centuries later than 300 BCE.

Corrected the page: the sentence stands on page 25 of the Feminist Press edition edited by Myra Stark, in the third paragraph of the essay, not on page 74. Nightingale wrote Cassandra in 1852, had it privately printed in 1860, and it was first published in 1928 in Ray Strachey’s The Cause.

Auden in Brecht, Plays Volume One, Methuen, 1960. The line closes scene 2, The Noble Child; the flight into the mountains is scene 3.

unused.quote: The door itself / makes no promises. / It is only a door.
unused.source: Adrienne Rich, Prospective Immigrants Please Note, closing lines, Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law (Harper and Row, 1963)
unused.note: Corrected publisher: Harper and Row published the book in 1963 and Norton reissued it in 1967.

unused.quote: Never did eye see the sun unless it had first become sunlike, and never can the soul have vision of the First Beauty unless itself be beautiful.
unused.source: Plotinus, Enneads, I.6.9, On Beauty (trans. Stephen MacKenna, 1917)
unused.note: Verified in MacKenna 1917. A clarity line rather than a beginning line.

unused.quote: For to be possessed of a vigorous mind is not enough; the prime requisite is rightly to apply it.
unused.source: René Descartes, Discourse on the Method, Part I, first paragraph (trans. John Veitch, 1850)
unused.note: Verified in Veitch; the 1850 date is from memory, not from a scan. Right application of the mind: a clarity line.

unused.quote: The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.
unused.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, proposition 5.6 (trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922)
unused.note: Verified. Held because Wittgenstein can appear once in a month and proposition 7 is the stronger line for a quieter month.

unused.quote: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
unused.source: Francis Bacon, Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Of Studies (1625)
unused.note: Verified. Held only because Bacon lands in May with Read not to contradict; one person a month.

unused.quote: All men by nature desire to know.
unused.source: Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book I, ch. 1, 980a21 (trans. W. D. Ross, 1908)
unused.note: Verified opening of the Metaphysics. Held: all men by nature desire to know is the appetite for truth.

unused.quote: I can’t do much with my hands; so I will make a battering-ram of my head and make a way through this rough-and-tumble world.
unused.source: Louisa May Alcott, Her Life, Letters, and Journals, letter to her father of 29 November 1856, p. 89 (ed. Ednah D. Cheney, 1889)
unused.note: Corrected: this is not a journal entry of 1850. Cheney prints it in chapter five, Authorship, inside a letter written from Boston to her father on 29 November 1856, her twenty-fourth birthday, on page 89 of the Roberts Brothers edition. The tag becomes Correspondence. The wording is exact.

unused.quote: I will not be ‘famous’, ‘great’. I will go on adventuring, changing, opening my mind and my eyes, refusing to be stamped and stereotyped.
unused.source: Virginia Woolf, A Writer’s Diary, the entry of 29 October 1933 (ed. Leonard Woolf, Hogarth Press, 1953)
unused.note: Verified. Held for a later month.

unused.quote: I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will; which I now exert to leave you.
unused.source: Charlotte Brontë, Jane Eyre, vol. II, ch. 8 (ch. 23), the orchard at Thornfield (Jane Eyre) (Smith, Elder, 1847)
unused.note: Corrected: the proposal cut the sentence short and closed it with a full stop no edition prints. The 1847 Smith, Elder first edition, volume II, chapter VIII, runs on to which I now exert to leave you, with a semicolon before it. Held: Charlotte Bronte stands in July with Life.

unused.quote: But I ask no favors for my sex. I surrender not our claim to equality. All I ask of our brethren is, that they will take their feet from off our necks, and permit us to stand upright on that ground which God designed us to occupy.
unused.source: Sarah Moore Grimké, Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, Letter II, Woman Subject Only to God, p. 10 (Isaac Knapp, 1838)
unused.note: Verified. Held: the Correspondence lane took three and this one belongs with Fuller and Cooper.

unused.quote: We never know how high we are / Till we are called to rise; / And then, if we are true to plan, / Our statures touch the skies.
unused.source: Emily Dickinson, ‘We never know how high we are’ (Fr1197, J1176), Poems, Third Series, ed. Mabel Loomis Todd, Life XIV (1896)
unused.note: Corrected: Aspiration is Todd title, not Dickinson, so the poem is cited by first line and standard numbers. Held: Dickinson stands at two for the year and the last slot should be chosen deliberately.

unused.quote: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
unused.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series, Self-Reliance (James Munroe, 1841)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Trust thyself is self-reliance under pressure more than counsel from an elder.

unused.quote: As firmly cemented clam shells / Fall apart in autumn, / So I must take to the road again, / Farewell, my friends.
unused.source: Matsuo Bashō, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, the closing verse at Ogaki (trans. Nobuyuki Yuasa, 1966)

unused.quote: I had a farm in Africa, at the foot of the Ngong Hills.
unused.source: Isak Dinesen, Out of Africa, Book One, The Ngong Farm, the opening sentence (Putnam, 1937)

unused.quote: For nothing is fixed, forever and forever and forever, it is not fixed; the earth is always shifting, the light is always changing, the sea does not cease to grind down rock.
unused.source: James Baldwin, Nothing Personal, the closing passage (Atheneum, 1964)

unused.quote: The answer must be, I think, that beauty and grace are performed whether or not we will or sense them. The least we can do is try to be there.
unused.source: Annie Dillard, Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, chapter 1, Heaven and Earth in Jest (Harper’s Magazine Press, 1974)

unused.quote: Though a country be sundered, hills and rivers endure; / And spring comes green again to trees and grasses / Where petals have been shed like tears / And lonely birds have sung their grief.
unused.source: Du Fu, A Spring View, lines 1 to 4, The Jade Mountain, p. 148 (trans. Witter Bynner with Kiang Kang-hu, 1929)

unused.quote: But not because of its magnificence / Dear is the Casuarina to my soul: / Beneath it we have played; though years may roll, / O sweet companions, loved with love intense, / For your sakes, shall the tree be ever dear.
unused.source: Toru Dutt, Our Casuarina Tree, stanza 3, lines 1 to 5, Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan (Kegan Paul, Trench and Co., 1882)
unused.note: Corrected the locator. Each stanza of the poem runs to eleven lines and the quotation is only the first five of stanza three, so the locator now names those lines. The wording stands as printed, with the colon after soul and the comma after sakes.

unused.quote: Barrabás came to us by sea, the child Clara wrote in her delicate calligraphy.
unused.source: Isabel Allende, The House of the Spirits, chapter 1, the opening sentence (trans. Magda Bogin, 1985)
unused.note: Verified opening line in Bogin’s translation; it returns as the novel’s last line. Held for a month that can use a pure opening.

unused.quote: The butterfly counts not months but moments, / and has time enough.
unused.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Fireflies, p. 15 (Macmillan, New York, 1928)
unused.note: Corrected in re-verification to a page locator. Held: a two line poem about moments, for the month of passing things.

unused.quote: He could see plainly that she was not herself. That is, he could not see that she was becoming herself and daily casting aside that fictitious self which we assume like a garment with which to appear before the world.
unused.source: Kate Chopin, The Awakening, chapter XIX (1899)
unused.note: Verified in chapter XIX of 1899. Casting aside the fictitious self, which is a truth line held for want of a day.

unused.quote: Some men say an army of horse and some men say an army on foot and some men say an army of ships is the most beautiful thing on the black earth. But I say it is what you love.
unused.source: Sappho, If Not, Winter, Fragment 16, lines 1 to 4 (trans. Anne Carson, 2002)
unused.note: Carried from January, verified in Carson, p. 27. Before it lands, the four lines must be marked with slashes in Carson’s lineation, which nobody has yet checked against the page; it is carried as prose.

unused.quote: I did not care what it was all about. All I wanted to know was how to live in it. Maybe if you found out how to live in it you learned from that what it was all about.
unused.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book II, chapter 14 (Jake Barnes) (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1926)
unused.note: Verified in the Scribner text of 1926. Held: Jake wants to know how to live in it, which is a search for clarity.

unused.quote: I will mount a long wind some day and break the heavy waves / And set my cloudy sail straight and bridge the deep, deep sea.
unused.source: Li Bai, The Hard Road, closing couplet, The Jade Mountain, p. 70 (trans. Witter Bynner, 1929)
unused.note: Verified. One Bynner poem landed already and only one may stand in a month, and the hard road is a courage line.

unused.quote: The wide world is all about you: you can fence yourselves in, but you cannot for ever fence it out.
unused.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book I, chapter 3, Three is Company (George Allen and Unwin, 1954) (Gildor Inglorion)
unused.note: Verified with the two-word for ever. Tolkien’s small hands is already held for September, so this goes to July.

unused.quote: There is no foreign land; it is the traveller only that is foreign, and now and again, by a flash of recollection, lights up the contrasts of the earth.
unused.source: Robert Louis Stevenson, The Silverado Squatters, Part II, With the Children of Israel, chapter III, The Return (Chatto and Windus, 1883)
unused.note: Corrected: the sentence is in The Return, Part II. Held: it is the traveller only that is foreign is a correction of the eye, which is June.
